prize_parts.citation: For the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, reaching a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18 and opening a new regime of precision measurement and tests of fundamental physics.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B029, Katori and Ye. After the first round the case is stronger than it was, because the objections raised against it are about scope and wording and not about the science. The decisive idea is magic-wavelength trapping, which lets many neutral atoms be held in a lattice without Doppler or recoil shifts and without a trap-induced shift of the clock transition. That is a distinct invention from the comb (2005, readout) and from single-ion control (2012, where the clock gains come from one ion with limited statistics). The 10^-18 regime was reached and then reproduced and intercompared by laboratories without a common origin (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST), so maturity rests on measured numbers and not on a roadmap. For the chair's question on the citation, I would now build it on the invention and the demonstrated performance, and I would keep the tests of fundamental physics in the wording only as what the clocks already do (comparisons that constrain variation of constants, centimetre-scale gravitational redshift). I would keep the redefinition of the second out of it, as Johansson, Lindroth and Pearce ask. This is a shift from the redefinition-adjacent phrasing Kroll and I used in round 1, and I think it is the safer and more accurate wording. It is also the case I find easiest to state in the form I understand the prize to require: a discovery or invention, and the people responsible for the original work.
statement.case_against: The serious reservation remains overlap with 2005 and 2012, and I do not think it is fully dissolved by saying the lattice clock is a sibling achievement. A committee member could reasonably say that a clock that reads out through a comb and borrows laser-cooling and narrow-line spectroscopy is a refinement within one lineage. Second, a two-name credit simplifies a crowded field: Lemonde, Ludlow, Lisdat, Bloom, Hinkley and the Al+ ion-clock groups reached comparable accuracy, and Hall's wider environment and the comb users stand behind Ye's group. My answer is that the question the prize asks is who originated the idea and who first took it to the decisive performance, and that answer is Katori and Ye; the others reproduced and extended it. I accept that this is a judgement and not a proof. Finally, my own B010 remains a cleaner single invention than any clock claim, but with no support beyond me and with unresolved priority questions (Kazarinov and Suris, and the Bell Labs co-inventors), it would be wrong to carry it into a final position.

responses.point: Kroll holds that the lattice clock is a sibling achievement to ion clocks and would write tests of fundamental physics and a path to redefining the second into the citation, and he discloses a stay in John Hall's laboratory.
responses.response: On the science we agree, but I now part from him on the citation. I included new tests of fundamental physics in round 1 and I still think they are a legitimate consequence, but the redefinition of the second has not happened, and the chair's question shows that several colleagues would not let it carry the case. I would drop that phrase and keep only what the clocks have already demonstrated. On the disclosure, I think disclosure with weighing, not recusal, is the right treatment: the link is to Hall's environment, Hall was honoured for the comb and not for the lattice clock, and Lindroth, Johansson, Mehlig, Pearce and I reached B029 on independent grounds, several of us after changing our own first choices. The outcome does not depend on his vote.

responses.point: Lindroth says the citation should name the lattice clock concept and its realisation and not a record number that several species and groups also hold, and that waiting for a metrological decision is not a scientific criterion.
responses.response: I agree and it changes my wording. A bare 10^-18 figure invites the reply that Yb and Al+ clocks are at the same level; so the citation should lead with the invention and development of the optical lattice clock and use the precision as the demonstration. I also agree on waiting: whether a body of metrologists adopts a new definition is a consequence of the science and not part of it. Where I add something is on the scope of overlap. Her point that the comb is the readout and not the source of accuracy is correct, and it is the best answer I know to the 2005 objection; the 2012 objection is harder, and I would say so openly in the committee's own reasoning.

responses.point: Johansson moved from B018 to B029 and argues the prize should rest on demonstrated 10^-18 performance and intercomparisons, not on a pending redefinition; he also treats the split of B004 among Blais, Girvin, Schoelkopf and Wallraff as unresolved.
responses.response: His evidence standard is the one I prefer, and I now apply it to my own citation. I also agree that B004 is not ready to be a preferred part in 2026: the 2025 prize on circuits, and the fact that he and Lindroth chose different triples from the same five names, both argue for waiting. On B018 I have not changed my view that it should be a candidate for a later year, once the Wineland overlap and the NIST and Monroe credit can be argued explicitly. I note again that he is a Chalmers colleague, and I am weighing his view on its merits.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from his own first choice B039 to B029, but says he cannot judge how much of the 10^-18 result belongs to the lattice concept and how much to laser stabilisation and cavity engineering contributed by other groups.
responses.response: That is a fair question, and from my side as a microscopist I would answer it by separating the enabling and the originating step. The ultrastable laser and cavity work enabled every high-accuracy optical clock, including ion clocks, and so it cannot be what distinguishes the lattice clock. What distinguishes it is the magic-wavelength lattice that makes a large atom number compatible with a small systematic shift, and that is the step Katori proposed and Ye's group carried to the regime where relativistic and many-body effects appear in the clock itself. I accept that this leaves the laser groups as important contributors outside any two-name prize, but that is true of most instrument-driven prizes.

responses.point: Eriksson still prefers B035 but says his own ranking of B029 was too low and he would support it, while naming overlap with 2005 and 2012 as the main reservation and treating DMFT as the more fundamental idea.
responses.response: I welcome his willingness to support B029 and I agree that B035 is conceptually strong and mature. The difficulty he states himself, that Metzner and others fall outside three names, is exactly the attribution question I understand the prize to need answered, and B029 does not have that problem. His comparison of fundamentality is a fair one, but I would not rank by how fundamental the idea is in the abstract: a clock is a measurement achievement with a clean credit, and this year the committee can reach a bounded result. I would not close B035 for later years, if the infinite-dimension credit can be resolved.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, asks colleagues to test B029 as hard as any other case and asks whether B013 deserves a hearing, given that colleagues object mainly on credit, and he would stay out of any final decision on it.
responses.response: I have tested it against the three tests he cares about: reproduction by independent laboratories, a bounded idea, and a clean credit. It passes the first two clearly, and the third with the qualifications above. On B013 I do not want to dismiss it. The afterglow discovery is concrete and instrument-driven, and I think it will be honoured in time. My objection remains credit, not merit: Jan van Paradijs and the optical identification teams are outside the names, and I cannot see in the supplied material how X-ray localisation and optical redshift would be divided. If a later round shows a defensible division, I would reconsider it for a later year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the lattice clock as a distinct achievement from the 2012 ion-control prize, which I regard as the harder of the two overlap objections.
Whether other lattice-clock and ion-clock groups have a claim on the 10^-18 milestone that a two-name credit leaves out; I think the originating idea answers this but it is a judgement.
How the committee weighs the pending redefinition of the second; I now keep it out of the citation but others may regard it as relevant to timing.
For fallbacks, I have not settled the mechanism and early-credit questions for B031 (Cao and Fatemi are outside the names), and I have not examined the priority of B010 closely.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with Katori or Ye is apparent from my profile. I record again that Goran Johansson is a Chalmers colleague, and that I weigh his view on its merits. My professional proximity is to materials physics and electron microscopy, which touches B010 more than B029. On Kroll's disclosure, I regard it as a disclosure to be weighed and not as grounds for recusal, since the result does not depend on his view.
